data.title: Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program
data.description:
Hyundai is preparing a new generation of cheaper, faster-charging and longer-lasting batteries to underpin a massive global product offensive that will see more than 100 new or updated vehicles launched by the end of the decade.

The Korean auto giant has detailed an extensive battery development program that includes new in-house battery cells, a switch to significantly cheaper mid-nickel chemistry for upcoming EVs, smarter battery management and new technology designed to prevent thermal runaway spreading through a battery pack.

It comes as Hyundai prepares one of the largest product rollouts in its history, with more than 100 global launches and major model updates planned by 2030.

READ MORE: Revealed: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute tech will debut in Santa Fe SUV range extender
READ MORE: Hyundai Ioniq 3 priced: UK version of new EV rival for BYD and MG starts at $42,500 … that’s promising for Australia
READ MORE: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute delayed: It’s still coming to Australia but it could take until 2030 to get here

More than 18 will take Hyundai into new products or market segments and seven new vehicles are due within the next eight months alone.

The rollout will include conventional combustion-powered vehicles, hybrids, extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs) and battery-electric vehicles, with electrified models targeted to account for 60 per cent of Hyundai sales by 2030, up from 23 per cent in 2025.

Hyundai is targeting 5.55 million global vehicle sales and a six per cent global market share by the end of the decade.

Central to the technology push is Hyundai’s development of its own battery cells.

The company claims its new high-performance cells can produce more than twice the output of the high-nickel cells it has previously used while reducing charging time by 40 per cent.

The first application will be Hyundai’s new EREV powertrain arriving in the first half of 2027.

That system will initially appear in the new Santa Fe EREV, which Hyundai says will offer more than 600 miles – about 965km – of total driving range.

Hyundai says the EREV requires less than half the battery capacity of a comparable battery-electric vehicle while still providing equivalent battery performance and EV driving characteristics.

The technology is also significant for Australia because EREV is emerging as a leading candidate to power Hyundai’s upcoming body-on-frame midsize ute.

But Hyundai’s battery plans extend well beyond EREVs.

One of the biggest developments for conventional battery-electric vehicles will arrive from 2027.

Hyundai says EVs launching next year will adopt mid-nickel NCM – nickel-cobalt-manganese – battery cells that will reduce battery costs by around 30 per cent compared with the technology they replace.

Importantly, Hyundai claims the cheaper cells will maintain what it describes as “optimal performance” under real-world driving conditions.

The potential significance is substantial because the battery remains one of the most expensive individual components in an electric vehicle.

A 30 per cent reduction in battery cost does not mean the price of an entire Hyundai EV will fall by 30 per cent, but reducing the cost of the pack potentially gives the company much greater scope to lower vehicle prices – or fit larger batteries and more equipment without pushing prices higher.

It should also help Hyundai compete against the rapidly expanding number of lower-cost Chinese EV manufacturers.

The first models using the new mid-nickel batteries have not been identified.

However, they will arrive during an enormous expansion of Hyundai’s electrified range.

In Europe alone Hyundai plans to cover 85 per cent of the market with a fully electrified portfolio, including five new SUVs and light-commercial vehicles, while increasing annual EV sales from 116,000 in 2025 to more than 420,000 by 2030.

Hyundai isn’t concentrating purely on the chemistry inside the battery.

Software will increasingly be used to manage the battery throughout its working life.

Hyundai says an enhanced cloud-based battery management system (BMS) will extend the average life of its EV batteries by 20 per cent by 2028.

The system will monitor battery condition and use cloud connectivity to detect abnormalities in individual cells in real time.

That could have implications beyond how long owners can keep their cars.

Battery degradation and the cost of replacing an EV battery remain important considerations for used EV buyers, while improved battery longevity potentially increases residual values and extends the useful life of an electric vehicle.

Hyundai hasn’t detailed exactly how it has calculated its claimed 20 per cent average battery-life improvement or translated it into expected kilometres or years of service.

The other major component of Hyundai’s battery strategy is safety.

Hyundai has developed what it calls Thermal Runaway Protection (TRP), designed to prevent heat from a failing battery cell spreading into adjacent cells.

Thermal runaway occurs when a battery cell experiences an uncontrolled increase in temperature that can trigger further cells, potentially creating a chain reaction within the battery pack.

Rather than simply delaying the spread of heat, Hyundai claims its TRP system can block it at the source.

It combines a battery design that dissipates heat with barriers between individual cells intended to stop heat transfer.

Hyundai says the technology has been verified through more than 200 repeated tests using both prismatic and pouch-type NCM batteries.

The cloud-based BMS and TRP effectively provide two layers of defence.

The BMS is intended to detect abnormal behaviour early enough for preventative action to be taken, while TRP provides a physical defence against heat spreading if a cell does fail.

The new thermal-runaway technology will make its production debut with Genesis, with Hyundai’s roadmap identifying the upcoming electric GV90 flagship SUV as its first application.

The battery investment is part of a broader change in Hyundai’s electrification strategy.

Rather than relying exclusively on battery-electric vehicles, Hyundai is expanding across EVs, hybrids and EREVs as it pushes towards its 5.55-million annual sales target.

Among the models identified in the latest roadmap are the IONIQ 3, new-generation Tucson and Tucson Hybrid, Santa Fe EREV, a new electric SUV for India and new global and European B-segment SUVs.

Genesis will simultaneously expand beyond pure EVs with its first hybrid, the GV80 Hybrid, as well as an EREV SUV targeting more than 640 miles – around 1030km – of total range and the battery-electric GV90 flagship.

The post Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: BMW iX4 revealed: Neue Klasse electric coupe SUV confirmed for Australia from $103,900 with up to 828km range
data.description:
BMW’s first iX4 electric coupe SUV will arrive in Australia in the first quarter of 2027, bringing up to 828km of claimed driving range and a starting price of $103,900 before on-road costs.

Two dual-motor all-wheel-drive variants will be offered initially: the iX4 40 xDrive at $103,900 and the iX4 50 xDrive at $119,900.

An M60 xDrive performance flagship will join the Australian line-up later in 2027. BMW’s global press kit lists provisional outputs of 450kW and 875Nm, a 3.9-second 0-100km/h sprint and up to 777km of WLTP range from a 108.7kWh usable battery. Australian pricing has not been announced.

READ MORE: New BMW X5 revealed: The fifth-generation luxury SUV will include an iX5 EV for the first time
READ MORE: BMW M3 EV revealed! Stunning wide-hipped concept previews 750kW production Neue Klasse electric weapon
READ MORE: The iconic BMW 3 Series goes electric! Meet the 2027 Neue Klasse BMW i3 xDrive 50

The electric iX4 slots into similar price territory to the petrol-powered X4. Against the 2025 X4 list prices, the $103,900 iX4 40 xDrive is $6200 dearer than the X4 xDrive20i M Sport but $4500 cheaper than the xDrive30i M Sport. The $119,900 iX4 50 xDrive also undercuts the petrol six-cylinder X4 M40i by $17,300. All prices exclude on-road costs.

Logical rivals for the BMW iX4 include the Audi Q6 Sportback e-tron and Polestar 4 coupe, which also combine electric power with a sloping-roof SUV body. The Porsche Macan Electric and Mercedes-Benz GLC with EQ Technology provide alternatives for buyers considering a premium electric SUV, while the forthcoming iX4 M60 will target performance models such as the Audi SQ6 Sportback e-tron and Porsche Macan 4S Electric.

The iX4 is the third model built on BMW’s dedicated Neue Klasse electric architecture, following the iX3 SUV and i3 sedan, and extends the technology into a lower-roofed coupe SUV body.

It arrives amid a broader expansion of BMW’s electric range that also includes a confirmed i3 Touring wagon and the forthcoming iX5. The larger iX5 adopts Neue Klasse technology but uses an updated version of BMW’s existing CLAR platform.

The entry-level iX4 40 xDrive produces a combined 275kW and 520Nm, with BMW claiming a 5.6-second sprint from 0-100km/h.

Its 82.6kWh usable battery delivers up to 638km of WLTP range and supports DC charging at up to 300kW.

The iX4 50 xDrive increases outputs to 345kW and 645Nm, cutting the claimed 0-100km/h time to 4.9 seconds.

A larger 108.7kWh usable battery provides up to 828km of WLTP range, while maximum DC charging power rises to 400kW.

That gives the 50 xDrive the same battery capacity, power, torque and acceleration time as the equivalent iX3, but an extra 23km of maximum claimed range compared with the upright SUV’s 805km.

BMW claims both iX4 variants can recharge from 10 to 80 per cent in 21 minutes at a suitable high-power charger. Under ideal conditions, the 50 xDrive can add up to 387km of WLTP range in 10 minutes, while the 40 xDrive can add up to 301km.

Both models use an 800-volt electrical system and BMW’s sixth-generation eDrive technology, including cylindrical battery cells. The Australian technical specification table lists 22kW AC charging for both variants.

At that rate, BMW quotes a full recharge in four hours and 15 minutes for the 40 xDrive and five hours and 30 minutes for the 50 xDrive.

The global specification also lists bidirectional charging capability, including vehicle-to-load power at up to 3.7kW and vehicle-to-home and vehicle-to-grid operation at up to 11kW. BMW Australia has not confirmed which functions will be available locally.

The quoted driving ranges are maximum WLTP figures, with BMW warning that optional larger wheels reduce range.

Measuring 4782mm long, 1895mm wide and 1595mm high, the iX4 rides on a 2897mm wheelbase and has a claimed drag coefficient of 0.23.

Its sloping roofline is accompanied by a pronounced rear spoiler and slim horizontal rear lights, while the front combines BMW’s kidney grille and headlights into a single graphic treatment.

Boot capacity is 490 litres, expanding to 1600 litres with the rear seats folded. Another 58 litres of storage is available beneath the bonnet.

The coupe body carries a practicality penalty compared with the iX3, which offers a 520-litre boot and 1750 litres with its rear seats folded.

Both launch variants are rated to tow up to 2000kg braked in European specification, although an Australian towing figure has not been confirmed in the local release.

Australian standard equipment includes an M Sport package, 20-inch alloy wheels, adaptive M suspension, M Sport brakes and a panoramic glass sunroof.

Both variants also receive electrically adjustable front seats with memory, heated front and rear seats, a heated steering wheel, Harman Kardon audio, wireless phone charging and an automatic tailgate.

The cabin adopts BMW’s Panoramic iDrive system, combining a display projected across the lower section of the windscreen with a 17.9-inch central touchscreen and a multifunction steering wheel.

A 3D head-up display is also listed as standard in the Australian equipment schedule, along with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

Driver assistance includes adaptive cruise control, steering and lane control assistance, and Parking Assistant Plus.

BMW’s “Heart of Joy” computer coordinates the drive system, braking, energy recuperation and steering-related functions. The company claims regenerative braking can handle up to 98 per cent of braking in everyday driving.

The M60 adds an electronically controlled rear locking differential and specific chassis tuning, according to the global press kit. Final Australian equipment details are yet to be announced.

Options for the launch variants include a $3500 M Sport Pro package, $4000 leather upholstery and wheels up to 22 inches. Most metallic paint finishes cost $2000, while Frozen Space Silver costs $6000.

The iX4 will be built at BMW’s Debrecen factory in Hungary.

The post BMW iX4 revealed: Neue Klasse electric coupe SUV confirmed for Australia from $103,900 with up to 828km range appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Lexus TZ confirmed for Australia: Three-row electric SUV to take on Kia EV9 and Volvo EX90 in 2027
data.description:
Toyota-owned Japanese luxury brand Lexus has confirmed its new TZ three-row electric SUV will launch in Australia in 2027, adding a larger family model to its battery-electric line-up.

The Australian commitment follows the earlier announcement of right-hand-drive production, which put the luxury SUV in contention for local sale but stopped short of confirming its arrival.

The TZ will compete with the Kia EV9 Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Volvo EX90, although Australian pricing, specifications and a more precise launch date have yet to be announced.

READ MORE: Just nine for Australia: Lexus RZ 600e performance flagship costs the same as original top-spec RZ
READ MORE: New Lexus NX confirmed for Australia: Plug-in hybrid SUV gets bigger battery, 100km-plus EV range and DC fast charging
READ MORE: New Lexus ES EV deep dive: World-first cabin tech, new operating system and safety technology that can call for help if its driver is incapacitated
READ MORE: Three-row Lexus TZ EV looking good for Australia: Kia EV9 and Volvo EX90 fighter to be built in right-hand drive

Local buyers will get an early opportunity to see the TZ at the 2026 Melbourne Cup Carnival, where it will be displayed alongside the limited-edition RZ 600e F Sport Performance at Lexus’s pavilion in the Birdcage Enclosure at Flemington Racecourse.

The TZ revealed overseas measures 5100mm long, 1990mm wide and 1705mm tall, with a 3050mm wheelbase. Its cabin has six seats arranged in three rows of two, including individual second-row seats with heating, ventilation and ottoman-style leg rests.

Previously announced overseas specifications include a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain producing 300kW, a 95.8kWh battery and a claimed driving range of up to 530km on the WLTP test cycle.

Lexus claims a 0-100km/h acceleration time of 5.4 seconds. DC charging peaks at 150kW, with a claimed 10-80 per cent recharge taking 35 minutes. Those figures have yet to be confirmed for the Australian version.

The overseas model also features rear-wheel steering, a 14.5-inch infotainment touchscreen and a 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster. Boot capacity is quoted at 290 litres with all six seats in use, expanding to 2017 litres with the second and third rows folded.

Lexus Australia chief executive Jack Hobbs said the two electric SUVs would serve different roles in the brand’s range.

“The all-new TZ and RZ 600e F SPORT Performance showcase the duality of Lexus electrification. One expands luxury through space and versatility; the other pushes the boundaries of thrilling performance.”

The RZ 600e F Sport Performance is due locally in late 2026, with just nine examples allocated to Australia.

Already priced at $135,000 before on-road costs, it sits above the RZ 500e Luxury and Sports Luxury and RZ 550e F Sport in the updated electric SUV range.

The 600e combines a 77kWh battery with a 313kW dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain. Lexus claims 0-100km/h in 4.4 seconds and up to 420km of WLTP range.

Its changes include sports suspension lowered by 20mm, additional aerodynamic components, unique 21-inch wheels and a yoke-style steering wheel paired with steer-by-wire technology.

The post Lexus TZ confirmed for Australia: Three-row electric SUV to take on Kia EV9 and Volvo EX90 in 2027 appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Nissan Navara Pro deep dive: How Aussie towing and touring needs prompted an upgrade to Nissan’s first PHEV ute
data.description:
Nissan has selected a larger petrol engine for its Australian-bound Navara Pro plug-in hybrid ute after testing two powertrains against local towing, load-carrying and long-distance driving requirements.

The China-built dual-cab, previously revealed internationally as the Frontier Pro, will arrive in Australia in 2027 with a 2.0-litre turbo-petrol engine rather than the 1.5-litre unit announced for the global model.

Nissan says the decision followed an Australian development program that has also assessed different rear suspension systems, differential-lock configurations, tyres and driver-assistance settings.

READ MORE: Frontier Pro becomes Navara Pro: Nissan confirms China-built PHEV ute for Australia with 300kW and 3.5-tonne towing
READ MORE: Nissan Pixo revealed: Here’s another cool European EV that looks set to bypass Australia
READ MORE: Nissan unveils two PHEV concepts in Beijing, including a 4×4 Toyota Prado rival already under study for Australia

The result will be an Oceania-specific version of Nissan’s first plug-in hybrid ute, entering a growing field of competitors including the BYD Shark 6, Ford Ranger PHEV, GWM Cannon and Cannon Alpha PHEVs, JAC Hunter and forthcoming Chery Stockman.

The local powertrain pairs the 2.0-litre turbo-petrol engine with an electric motor integrated into an eight-speed automatic transmission. Preliminary combined outputs are 300kW and 800Nm, subject to final homologation.

Nissan is also targeting up to 1000kg of payload and a 3500kg braked towing capacity, although both figures remain subject to final approval.

According to the company, towing, payload and sustained performance were central to the decision to choose the larger engine after evaluating both PHEV systems.

However, Nissan has not released comparative test results for the two powertrains, so the announcement does not establish how much the 2.0-litre system improves performance under load.

“Australia wasn’t simply where we tested Navara Pro PHEV. It was one of the markets helping shape it,” Nissan Oceania managing director Steve Milette said.

“The depth of local evaluation and the collaboration between our teams in Australia, Japan and China reflect the importance of Oceania to the development of this vehicle.”

The first prototypes arrived in Australia in 2025. Five development and prototype vehicles have since been brought here, collectively covering more than 20,000km, with testing continuing.

Nissan Australia has worked with teams from Japan and Zhengzhou Nissan in China, feeding local findings into the vehicle’s development.

The program extends beyond the engine choice. Nissan says it has evaluated and refined suspension, driver-assistance calibration, terrain and drive modes, tyres, towing and load performance.

One significant decision remains unresolved: whether Australian buyers will get leaf springs or a multi-link coil-spring rear suspension.

Nissan has assessed both configurations and says the final Australian suspension specification will be announced closer to the start of sales.

That choice will be relevant to buyers weighing ride comfort against load-carrying requirements, although spring type alone does not determine either.

The Navara Pro will use a mechanical four-wheel-drive system, with low-range capability and mechanical differential locks.

Nissan says its local program has tested front, rear and combined differential-lock configurations. It has not yet confirmed which arrangement will reach Australian showrooms.

Four drive modes — Eco, Standard, Sport and Slippery — and seven terrain modes are listed. The latter comprise Standard, Deep Snow, Mud, Sand, Rock, Wading and Expert.

Nissan says the modes adjust powertrain, steering and traction-control settings, with the systems evaluated and tuned for Australian and New Zealand conditions.

Vehicle-to-load functionality will also be available, allowing the ute to supply electrical power for work or recreational use. Its maximum output has not been announced.

The larger engine and targeted towing and payload figures address key Australian ute requirements, but important details about the plug-in system remain outstanding.

Nissan has yet to disclose the local battery capacity, electric-only driving range, charging rates or fuel consumption. The overseas Frontier Pro’s previously announced range figures therefore should not be assumed to apply to the Australian version.

For buyers planning regular towing or remote touring, fuel use after the battery’s initial charge has been depleted will also be relevant. Nissan has not supplied that figure or published loaded towing results.

Australia and New Zealand will be the first right-hand-drive markets to receive the Navara Pro PHEV. Pricing, final equipment and a precise Australian launch date will be announced closer to its arrival in 2027.

The post Nissan Navara Pro deep dive: How Aussie towing and touring needs prompted an upgrade to Nissan’s first PHEV ute appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: EV sales more than double as Tesla, BYD and Geely help electric cars outsell petrol again in September
data.description:
Battery electric vehicles have outsold petrol-powered vehicles in Australia for a second consecutive month, with September deliveries more than doubling compared with a year ago.

Australians took delivery of 26,287 battery electric vehicles during the month, up 117.7 per cent and accounting for 24.2 per cent of the new-vehicle market.

That compares with an 11.3 per cent share in September 2025, underlining how quickly EVs are gaining ground as more brands and models enter the market.

READ MORE: New findings: Australia’s EV boom is reshaping the used car market as record sales feed future supply
READ MORE: EVs outsell diesel and hybrids for the first time as new-car market smashes all-time record; Tesla, BYD booming
READ MORE: Record sales for Tesla! EV heavyweight has huge May – Tesla Model Y outsells Ford Ranger, Toyota Hilux, Toyota RAV4

Battery electric vehicles narrowly outnumbered petrol vehicles, which recorded 26,018 sales, and also finished ahead of diesels on 25,173.

The figures combine the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries’ VFACTS report with Tesla and Polestar deliveries reported separately through the Electric Vehicle Council.

Together, the two reporting sources recorded 108,778 new-vehicle deliveries in September, up 1.8 per cent year-on-year. The VFACTS-only total was 102,924, an increase of 0.9 per cent.

The modest overall market growth contrasts with the much stronger increase in EV deliveries, while petrol sales fell 36.2 per cent and diesel sales declined 18.4 per cent.

EVs have now accounted for 180,591 deliveries during the first nine months of 2026, representing 18.9 per cent of the market compared with 8.1 per cent at the same point last year.

September’s share was slightly below August’s 24.9 per cent, but remained well above the year-to-date average.

Three battery electric SUVs finished among Australia’s 10 best-selling vehicles in September.

The Tesla Model Y led the EV field with 4476 deliveries, placing it third overall behind the Ford Ranger on 5062 and Toyota RAV4 on 4624, but ahead of the Toyota HiLux on 4455.

The BYD Sealion 7 finished fifth with 2687 deliveries, while the Geely EX5 placed eighth with 2008.

According to the Electric Vehicle Council, Tesla delivered 5654 vehicles in September, up 21.3 per cent, placing it sixth among all brands.

The Model Y’s monthly result was up 14 per cent, with the six-seat Model Y L contributing 1764 deliveries to the SUV’s total.

Model Y deliveries have reached 35,930 for the year, up 108.4 per cent compared with the first nine months of 2025.

The Tesla Model 3 added 1178 September deliveries, up 60.1 per cent. Its year-to-date total of 5775 was up a more modest 6.6 per cent.

Together, the two model families took Tesla’s nine-month total to 41,705 deliveries, an increase of 84.1 per cent.

BYD remained Australia’s second-largest vehicle brand overall, delivering 8191 vehicles across its battery electric and plug-in hybrid ranges, up 61.1 per cent.

Market leader Toyota also recorded growth in its electric offering, with the bZ4X delivering a record monthly result of 410 sales in September. Toyota said year-to-date sales were nearly five times higher than at the same point in 2025, following an upgrade late last year and the addition of the Touring variant in mid-2026.

Toyota said plug-in hybrids had accounted for approximately 30 per cent of new-generation RAV4 sales since its June launch. The RAV4 recorded 4624 deliveries across its range in September, with a cheaper GXL 2WD PHEV variant due in the first quarter of 2027.

Geely delivered 4473 vehicles across its electric and plug-in hybrid line-up. Alongside the EX5, its smaller EX2 electric car contributed 1211 deliveries.

Electric-only sister brand Zeekr recorded 2050 deliveries, compared with 120 a year earlier, marking its third consecutive month above 2000.

The Zeekr 7X accounted for 1628 September deliveries and led the VFACTS medium SUV category priced above $65,000, with a 28.8 per cent share. That ranking excludes Tesla, which reports separately through the Electric Vehicle Council. The Model Y remained the stronger seller with 4476 deliveries.

Plug-in hybrids also continued to expand rapidly, with September deliveries rising 122.7 per cent to 10,072. Conventional hybrids increased 20.7 per cent to 17,843.

Combined, battery electric vehicles and PHEVs accounted for 33.4 per cent of September deliveries. Adding conventional hybrids took the electrified share to 49.8 per cent.

FCAI acting chief executive Dianne O’Hara said greater choice and competition were supporting the changing sales mix.

“Australian motorists are embracing a broader range of powertrains, following greater model choice offered by manufacturers and growing competition,” she said.

GWM provided another example of the broadening electrified market, reporting 609 deliveries of its Ora 5 electric SUV.

The company said its battery electric sales increased 542 per cent, while its hybrid and PHEV sales grew 26 per cent and 109 per cent respectively.

GWM delivered 5212 vehicles overall, up 5.4 per cent. That placed it sixth in VFACTS, or seventh when Tesla was included.

The National Automotive Leasing and Salary Packaging Association attributed some of the EV growth to household budget pressures and buyers seeking less exposure to fluctuating fuel prices.

Chief executive Rohan Martin said the Electric Car Discount was helping make the initial switch affordable for working Australians.

“An EV can deliver substantial savings on running costs, but households first need to be able to afford the switch. That is where the Electric Car Discount continues to make a real difference,” he said.

Martin said households with rooftop solar could also reduce transport costs by charging with electricity generated at home.

While petrol and diesel vehicles remain ahead over the first nine months of the year, September’s result shows battery electric vehicles sustaining a much larger presence in the Australian market than a year ago.

The post EV sales more than double as Tesla, BYD and Geely help electric cars outsell petrol again in September appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: VW Mission Efficiency Deep Dive: Here’s how Volkswagen squeezed extraordinary EV range from just 54.9kWh
data.description:
Electric car makers have increasingly turned to bigger batteries to deliver longer driving ranges, but Volkswagen’s remarkable Mission Efficiency prototype demonstrates there’s another way.

The German brand’s ultra-slippery experimental EV has recorded average energy consumption of just 6.89kWh/100km during a 1278km European road trip, despite carrying a relatively modest 54.9kWh usable battery.

For some perspective, plenty of contemporary electric cars consume somewhere in the teens of kWh/100km, while larger and heavier electric SUVs can easily venture beyond 20kWh/100km.

READ MORE: 6.48kWh/100km! Volkswagen Mission Efficiency electric car shows how frugal an EV can be in the real world
READ MORE: Global unveiling: After many teases, the VW ID. Polo has been revealed in full. Is this the best small EV in the world?
READ MORE: Volkswagen turns iconic GTI on its head: Electric ID.3 is first rear-drive GTI and the most powerful ever

Volkswagen’s answer isn’t one breakthrough technology. Instead, it has attacked virtually everything that consumes or wastes energy, from aerodynamics and tyre resistance to braking, weight, climate control and even the stereo.

And much of what sits underneath the Mission Efficiency isn’t experimental.

Its 99kW front-mounted electric motor and battery are derived from the technology developed for the new Volkswagen ID. Polo, while the underlying front-wheel-drive MEB+ architecture will underpin a new generation of relatively affordable Volkswagen EVs.

That makes the Mission Efficiency an intriguing demonstration of how much further an EV might travel if engineers concentrate on reducing its energy requirement rather than simply adding more battery.

Aerodynamics

The Mission Efficiency’s most spectacular number is its drag coefficient of just 0.158.

But drag coefficient is only part of the equation. The VW also has a small frontal area of 2.08 square metres, helped by its unusually low 1392mm overall height.

Its body then progressively narrows towards the rear in the classic aerodynamic teardrop or ‘boat-tail’ shape.

Volkswagen has attacked the airflow in less obvious places too.

The underbody is almost completely enclosed, the rear wheels are covered and three active cooling flaps in the nose remain closed when cooling air isn’t required.

The doors use frameless windows and flush handles, while the rear axle has even been narrowed compared with the ID. Polo to help clean up airflow beneath the car.

The benefits increase dramatically with speed because aerodynamic drag becomes an increasingly important component of a vehicle’s total energy requirement.

Volkswagen claims the Mission Efficiency consumes more than 30 per cent less energy than an ID. Polo once speeds exceed 80km/h.

The most telling comparison comes at German autobahn speeds: VW says driving the Mission Efficiency at about 140km/h requires roughly the same amount of energy as driving an ID. Polo at 100km/h.

Wheels

One of the more fascinating lessons from the project concerns wheels.

Volkswagen estimates they are responsible for between 25 and 30 per cent of a vehicle’s aerodynamic resistance.

So rather than simply fitting conventional aero wheel covers, its engineers worked on controlling airflow both around and through them.

The front wheelarches sit closely around the tyres to reduce turbulence, while the rear wheels are completely enclosed.

VW has also developed patented deflectors mounted on the inside of all four wheels. Their job is to prevent air entering the rims and creating turbulence. Flat external wheel covers complete the package.

Then there are the tyres themselves. Volkswagen worked with Continental to develop special tyres based on its production EcoContact 7.

Their claimed rolling resistance is just 4.9kg per tonne, around 25 per cent below the threshold required to achieve the European Union’s highest Class A tyre rating.

Battery

Mission Efficiency’s battery is particularly interesting because its capacity is nothing extraordinary. It contains 54.9kWh of usable energy – less than many mainstream EVs.

It uses NMC lithium-ion chemistry and cell-to-pack construction, eliminating conventional intermediate battery modules by integrating cells more directly into the pack.

The battery is related to the production unit developed for the ID. Polo, although Volkswagen unlocked an additional 2.9kWh of usable capacity through software for Mission Efficiency.

Maximum DC charging power is 105kW and AC charging is rated at 11kW. Those aren’t headline-grabbing charging figures. The point is that Mission Efficiency needs relatively little electricity in the first place.

Its official WLTP energy consumption is just 8.4kWh/100km. During Volkswagen’s documented 1278.36km journey from Wolfsburg in Germany to Vienna in Austria, that fell to 6.89kWh/100km excluding charging losses, or 7.51kWh/100km when those losses were included.

The battery required only one recharge during the journey and VW says the car arrived with another 164km of indicated range remaining.

A separate idealised test at a constant 68km/h, without gradients and with energy consumers such as air-conditioning switched off, produced an even lower 6.48kWh/100km.

Braking

Another potential pointer towards future production EVs is hidden in the braking system.

Mission Efficiency retains conventional hydraulic brakes at the front but uses a new electromechanical brake at the rear, developed jointly by Volkswagen and automotive technology company Aumovio.

Rather than hydraulic pressure activating the rear brakes, electrical actuators do the job. That eliminates rear hydraulic lines and brake fluid while reducing mechanical friction losses.

More importantly for an EV, Volkswagen says the system enables variable brake-force distribution and can improve the interaction between friction braking and regenerative braking.

That potentially allows more of the vehicle’s kinetic energy to be recovered and returned to the battery rather than disappearing as heat through the brakes.

Solar

There is also a 370-watt photovoltaic system integrated into the glass roof and rear section of the Mission Efficiency.

Volkswagen says it can contribute the equivalent of up to 30km of extra range per day, depending heavily on location, weather and season.

But that needs some qualification. The solar cells aren’t intended to transform Mission Efficiency into a solar-powered EV. They feed the vehicle’s electrical system and reduce the amount of energy ancillary systems need to draw from the traction battery.

It’s another example of the philosophy behind the entire car: rather than finding one enormous energy saving, VW has accumulated lots of smaller ones.

Air-conditioning

Climate control can take a significant bite out of an EV’s available energy, particularly when heating the cabin in cold conditions.

Mission Efficiency therefore uses a heat pump to reduce the electrical energy required for heating. The system uses R744 – carbon dioxide – as its refrigerant rather than a conventional synthetic refrigerant.

Volkswagen has applied the same energy-saving philosophy elsewhere inside. There’s no conventional infotainment screen. Instead, occupants bring a smartphone or tablet.

Even conventional permanently installed speakers have been deleted and replaced by a portable Bluetooth speaker.

Weight

The Mission Efficiency combines elements of the ID. Polo structure with a self-supporting aluminium construction, while the doors, bonnet, tailgate, guards and other components employ carbon-fibre and aramid composite materials.

That part of the formula is clearly less representative of an affordable production EV than its motor and battery technology, because extensive lightweight composites remain expensive.

Nevertheless, it illustrates the engineering trade-off inherent in long-range EVs.

Adding battery capacity increases range, but also adds weight. That additional weight then requires more energy to accelerate and move, potentially requiring still more battery capacity.

Mission Efficiency attacks the problem from the opposite direction.

Mirrors

There’s even an interesting lesson in something Volkswagen decided not to fit.

Despite the extreme aerodynamic focus, Mission Efficiency retains conventional exterior mirrors rather than replacing them with cameras.

Volkswagen says wind-tunnel development showed the overall aerodynamic benefit from camera mirrors would have been relatively small.

They would also have added cost and consumed electricity.

It’s a tiny detail, but one that neatly sums up the project: a technology doesn’t automatically make the car more efficient simply because it looks more advanced.

What are the implications for future VW EVs?

Don’t expect an ID. Polo with covered rear wheels, carbon-fibre body panels and a Cd of 0.158. Mission Efficiency is a technology demonstrator rather than a preview of a production model.

But its significance is that the fundamental electrical hardware isn’t exotic.

The 99kW APP290 permanent-magnet motor, battery technology and front-wheel-drive MEB+ architecture have strong links with Volkswagen’s new generation of production EVs.

Other technologies – active cooling flaps, improved underbody aerodynamics, lower-resistance tyres, smarter thermal management, reduced brake drag and better wheel aerodynamics – are far more transferable to everyday cars than Mission Efficiency’s dramatic body shape suggests.

And that’s perhaps the most important lesson from the project. The industry’s EV range battle has often focused on how many kilowatt-hours can be squeezed beneath a vehicle.

Mission Efficiency demonstrates the other side of the equation. Make an electric car require substantially fewer kilowatt-hours to travel each 100km and suddenly a relatively modest battery can take you a very long way.

The post VW Mission Efficiency Deep Dive: Here’s how Volkswagen squeezed extraordinary EV range from just 54.9kWh appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Radical Jaguar Type 01 revealed: 757kW electric GT confirmed for Australia from about $300,000
data.description:
Jaguar has revealed the production Type 01 electric grand tourer, confirming its radical four-door flagship will be offered in Australia with pricing starting at approximately $300,000 plus on-road costs.

Australian orders will open in 2027, although the British brand has yet to announce exact local ordering or delivery dates.

Unveiled in New York, the Type 01 is the first production model in Jaguar’s reinvention as an electric-only luxury brand, bringing a three-motor powertrain, up to 720km of claimed WLTP range and styling that carries key elements of the dramatic Type 00 concept into production.

READ MORE: Jaguar’s wild new EV interior revealed: Type 01 takes radical concept cabin into production
READ MORE: Jaguar’s radical new EV named: Production badge is the least outrageous bit of this Rolls-Royce-rivalling limo
READ MORE: Jaguar shows off Type 00 testing, just days after rubbishing reports it’s walking back its EV-only commitment

It also represents a substantial move upmarket for Jaguar, with the indicative Australian starting price positioning the new GT well above its previous I-Pace electric SUV.

The Type 01 is designed, engineered and built in the UK on the new Jaguar Electric Architecture, or JEA, developed specifically for the brand’s next generation of EVs.

Jaguar claims combined outputs of up to 757kW and 1365Nm, making the Type 01 its most powerful production road car.

The all-wheel drive system combines a 260kW front motor with two 310kW rear motors. Those individual motor ratings do not represent the car’s combined system output, which Jaguar quotes at 757kW.

The claimed 0-100km/h acceleration time is 3.2 seconds, while Jaguar says the Type 01 can accelerate from 100-180km/h in four seconds.

Its two rear motors allow torque to be varied between the rear wheels to assist handling, while the powertrain can disconnect the rear motors when their performance is not required, such as during highway cruising.

A lithium-ion battery with 118kWh of usable capacity supplies the motors, with Jaguar quoting up to 720km of WLTP range and an anticipated US EPA range of up to 643km.

The company separately claims up to 515km at a constant 120km/h. That highway figure is a manufacturer claim under specified conditions, rather than a guarantee of Australian touring range.

The Type 01 uses an 850-volt electrical architecture and supports DC fast charging at up to 350kW.

Jaguar says a suitable charger can replenish the battery from 10 to 80 per cent in approximately 22 minutes, or add up to 321km of claimed range in 13 minutes.

A split-charging system also allows charging at up to 250kW from compatible 400-volt equipment.

AC charging capability extends to 22kW, with an unusual arrangement providing an AC charging port on each side of the car to make plugging in easier.

Jaguar says details of Australian home and public charging support will be announced closer to the local launch.

Measuring 5235mm long and just 1403mm tall, the Type 01 retains the concept’s long bonnet, low roofline and substantial rear overhang, although the production car has four doors rather than the Type 00’s two.

Standard wheels measure 23 inches, with 21-inch alternatives available.

The rear also retains a particularly unconventional feature: there is no rear window. Instead, a rear-facing camera supplies a digital display positioned centrally at the base of the windscreen, replacing a conventional interior mirror.

Jaguar quotes a drag coefficient of 0.23, aided by active cooling vanes and a three-stage deployable rear spoiler.

Underneath, the chassis combines double-wishbone front suspension, an integral-link rear arrangement, air springs with switchable volume and electronically controlled twin-valve dampers.

Rear-wheel steering provides up to six degrees of movement in the opposite direction to the front wheels at low speeds, contributing to a claimed 11.5-metre wall-to-wall turning circle.

At higher speeds, the rear wheels steer in the same direction as the fronts to improve stability. Jaguar also quotes a 50:50 weight distribution.

Inside, the Type 01 has four seats separated by a central spine running through the cabin, with brass-effect aluminium detailing repeated along the doors.

The production dashboard incorporates a 24-inch OLED display ahead of the driver and extending towards the centre of the car, plus a seven-inch touchscreen for frequently used functions such as climate and audio controls.

Rear passengers have their own seven-inch control screen, while wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are standard.

The front seats offer electric adjustment, heating, cooling and massage functions, while the rear seats are heated and cooled.

A switchable panoramic glass roof is also standard, along with a Meridian-developed 38-speaker audio system incorporating a 13-speaker soundbar across the dashboard.

Despite its low roofline and four-seat layout, Jaguar says the powered tailgate opens onto more than 450 litres of luggage space, increasing to 1000 litres with the rear seats folded.

A launch specification called Design Vision will feature satin silver paint, specific 23-inch wheels and brass-effect exterior detailing.

Jaguar will also offer a Chromatic Moments collection limited to 60 vehicles globally, with a choice of specially developed French Ultramarine or London Red paint. Australian allocations have not been announced.

Globally, orders are scheduled to open in early 2027, with first customer deliveries expected in the second half of the year and UK pricing starting at £130,000.

The post Radical Jaguar Type 01 revealed: 757kW electric GT confirmed for Australia from about $300,000 appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: BMW’s fuel cell iX5 aims for 750km range, sub-five-second 0-100km/h and sub-five-minute refuelling
data.description:
BMW’s first production hydrogen fuel-cell electric vehicle is targeting up to 750km range, a sub-five-second 0-100km/h sprint and sub-five-minute refuelling, but the German brand has confirmed there are currently no plans to bring it to Australia.

The BMW iX5 Hydrogen is progressing through vehicle testing and manufacturing preparations ahead of a planned 2028 production start.

It will complete a global five-powertrain line-up for the new-generation X5, joining battery-electric, plug-in hybrid, petrol and diesel versions.

READ MORE: 2026 BMW iX3 50 xDrive Review: Our first Australian test proves the hype is real! The all-new iX3 EV is a great drive with a huge real-world range.
READ MORE: New BMW X5 revealed: The fifth-generation luxury SUV will include an iX5 EV for the first time
READ MORE: BMW M3 EV revealed! Stunning wide-hipped concept previews 750kW production Neue Klasse electric weapon

Australia will take the other four powertrain types, with BMW’s local operation pointing to the ownership experience and supporting infrastructure as the reasons hydrogen remains outside its plans.

“BMW’s approach is always driven by the customer ownership experience. While the BMW iX5 Hydrogen has been confirmed globally for series production, there are currently no plans for Australia,” BMW Australia said.

“For any new technology to be successful, customers need confidence that the supporting ecosystem, including refuelling infrastructure and service support, is in place.

“At present our focus for the new X5 for the Australian market will comprise the combustion engine (petrol and diesel), plug-in hybrid and fully electric models.

“The combustion engine variants will go on sale this quarter followed by the electric and plug-in variants in H1 2027.”

The new diesel X5 40d xDrive is priced from $143,900 before on-road costs, while the petrol X5 40 xDrive starts at $145,900. Both feature six-cylinder engines and 48-volt mild-hybrid technology.

The battery-electric iX5 60 and plug-in hybrid X5 50e will broaden the Australian range next year.

For the hydrogen version, BMW’s latest development work centres on the interaction between its fuel-cell system, electric motor, high-voltage battery, hydrogen tanks and control electronics.

Engineers are testing the integrated system under demanding environmental conditions and high loads, while also developing its efficiency and driving dynamics.

BMW is targeting a 0-100km/h time of less than five seconds, with performance intended to be on a par with the battery-electric iX5.

The claimed range of up to 750km on the WLTP cycle and refuelling time of less than five minutes also remain development targets. BMW says binding WLTP consumption figures are not yet available for the prototype.

The iX5 Hydrogen uses a third-generation fuel-cell system co-developed with Toyota.

Rather than burning hydrogen in a combustion engine, it combines hydrogen from its tanks with oxygen from the surrounding air in an electrochemical reaction that generates electricity for the electric drive system.

A high-voltage battery works alongside the fuel cell, while BMW’s Energy Master control unit manages the high-voltage system. BMW says the battery and electronics allow greater energy recovery under deceleration, improving overall efficiency.

Power and torque figures for the production model have not been announced in the latest update.

A significant change from BMW’s earlier hydrogen prototypes is the new Hydrogen Flat Storage system.

Previously detailed by BMW, it comprises seven interconnected carbon-fibre composite tanks housed in a metal frame, storing around seven kilograms of hydrogen at 700 bar.

The flat arrangement occupies the installation space used by the battery-electric model’s high-voltage battery, preserving cabin space and allowing the hydrogen version to share a production line with other X5 powertrains.

Sharing components, packaging and manufacturing processes is central to BMW’s efforts to reduce the cost of fuel-cell vehicles. www.bmwgroup.com

Alongside vehicle testing, BMW is beginning another prototype assembly phase for the fuel-cell system at its Hydrogen Competence Centre in Munich.

The earlier phase concentrated on component manufacturing feasibility and initial supplier qualification. The next stage focuses on validating testing methods and preparing manufacturing processes for series production.

BMW’s Steyr engine plant in Austria will produce the fuel-cell systems. Initial test benches and manufacturing equipment have already been installed, with staff training underway.

Additional system components are being manufactured at BMW’s Landshut facility in Germany.

The production program represents a substantial step beyond the two previous-generation iX5 Hydrogen prototypes BMW brought to Australia in 2024 for testing and demonstration duties.

Those vehicles were part of a global pilot fleet of almost 100 examples. When EV Central’s Bruce Newton drove one at the Lang Lang proving ground in Victoria, BMW was still considering whether to approve a production fuel-cell vehicle. www.carsales.com.au

The X5 has since been selected and production scheduled for 2028. But while BMW continues to develop hydrogen as an alternative electric powertrain globally, its Australian X5 expansion will focus on battery-electric and plug-in hybrid models.

The post BMW’s fuel cell iX5 aims for 750km range, sub-five-second 0-100km/h and sub-five-minute refuelling appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Frontier Pro becomes Navara Pro: Nissan confirms China-built PHEV ute for Australia with 300kW and 3.5-tonne towing
data.description:
Nissan’s China-built Frontier Pro plug-in hybrid ute will arrive in Australia in 2027 wearing the Navara Pro badge, with a locally selected 2.0-litre turbo-petrol powertrain, claimed 3500kg towing capacity and up to one tonne of payload.

The five-seat dual-cab will be Nissan Australia’s first plug-in hybrid, joining an increasingly crowded ute segment that includes the BYD Shark 6, Ford Ranger PHEV, GWM Cannon and Cannon Alpha PHEVs and JAC Hunter.

Chery’s diesel-electric Stockman is also scheduled to begin Australian customer deliveries in February 2027, adding another competitor before the Nissan arrives.

READ MORE: Nissan Pixo revealed: Here’s another cool European EV that looks set to bypass Australia
READ MORE: Nissan unveils two PHEV concepts in Beijing, including a 4×4 Toyota Prado rival already under study for Australia
READ MORE: Range extender overhaul: Nissan Qashqai goes all e-POWER for 2026 as pricing shifts upward

Nissan has yet to announce pricing, a precise launch date, battery capacity, electric-only range or charging specifications. Australia and New Zealand will be the first right-hand-drive markets to receive the electrified ute.

The Navara Pro is the vehicle previously revealed internationally as the Frontier Pro, developed and built in China through Zhengzhou Nissan, Nissan’s joint venture with Dongfeng. It is a separate vehicle from the Mitsubishi Triton-based diesel Navara currently sold in Australia.

Importantly, the Australian version will differ from the 1.5-litre turbo-petrol PHEV specification announced at the Frontier Pro’s Shanghai motor show debut.

Nissan says local testing of both that drivetrain and a new 2.0-litre alternative led it to select the larger engine for Australia and New Zealand, particularly to meet towing, payload and sustained-performance requirements.

The Oceania powertrain combines the 2.0-litre turbo-petrol engine with an electric motor integrated into an eight-speed automatic transmission.

Preliminary combined outputs are 300kW and 800Nm, subject to final homologation.

That matches the GWM Cannon Alpha PHEV’s 300kW while exceeding its 750Nm torque claim. The smaller Cannon Hi4-T produces 310kW and 750Nm, while the Ford Ranger PHEV develops 207kW and 697Nm.

BYD’s Shark 6 Premium produces 321kW and 650Nm, while the Performance delivers 350kW and 700Nm. The Nissan therefore has less claimed power than either BYD, but more torque.

Chery quotes 350kW and 800Nm for the forthcoming Stockman, while JAC claims 360kW for its Hunter, placing the Nissan below the segment’s highest power outputs.

Nissan’s preliminary 3500kg braked towing capacity puts it alongside the Ranger PHEV, both GWM plug-in utes, JAC Hunter and Shark 6 Performance. The Shark 6 Premium retains a 2500kg limit, while Chery’s latest Stockman specifications list 3495kg.

The Nissan’s targeted payload of up to 1000kg would also be competitive. Published figures for rivals include 915kg for the JAC Hunter, 835kg for the Cannon Hi4-T, 790kg for the Shark 6 Premium and 685kg for the Cannon Alpha PHEV. Final Nissan figures and grade-by-grade capacities remain unconfirmed.

Electric driving range remains a significant unanswered question. The overseas Frontier Pro’s previously publicised 135km claim should not be treated as an Australian specification, given the different powertrain and the absence of a confirmed local battery or test-cycle figure.

The Navara Pro will use mechanical four-wheel drive, with low-range capability and differential locks.

Nissan says it has evaluated front, rear and combined differential-lock configurations, but has not yet confirmed the final Australian arrangement. Leaf-spring and multi-link coil-spring rear suspension systems have also been tested, with the production choice still to be announced.

Five development and prototype vehicles have been brought to Australia since 2025, collectively covering more than 20,000km so far.

The program has assessed powertrains, suspension, driver-assistance calibration, tyres, drive modes, towing and load carrying, with input from Nissan teams in Australia, Japan and China.

“Australia wasn’t simply where we tested Navara Pro PHEV. It was one of the markets helping shape it,” Nissan Oceania managing director Steve Milette said.

Four drive modes and seven terrain modes are listed, while vehicle-to-load capability will be available. Its electrical output has not been disclosed.

Depending on grade, equipment could include a large touchscreen, digital instrument display, panoramic sunroof and heated and ventilated front seats. Nissan has yet to confirm the Australian line-up or standard equipment.

The ute also advances Nissan Australia’s shift towards Chinese-developed vehicles, with further electrified SUVs and potentially sedans previously identified as part of its product expansion.

That direction comes as Nissan passes over European electric models such as the Renault-based Micra and Pixo, both of which have been ruled out for Australia despite right-hand-drive availability.

The Navara Pro will be eligible for Nissan’s service-activated warranty of up to 10 years or 300,000km, whichever comes first, when the required servicing is completed through authorised Nissan dealers. The underlying vehicle warranty is five years with unlimited kilometres.

The post Frontier Pro becomes Navara Pro: Nissan confirms China-built PHEV ute for Australia with 300kW and 3.5-tonne towing appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Australia has a new electric SUV pricing benchmark: Leapmotor B03X arrives from $29,990 drive-away
data.description:
Leapmotor has announced Australian pricing for its B03X small electric SUV, with a $29,990 drive-away starting price undercutting the BYD Atto 2 and establishing a new entry point for battery-powered SUVs.

Due in dealerships in November, the Chinese-built five-seater will be offered in two versions: the entry-level Style and the $33,990 drive-away Design LR, which adds a larger battery, more driving range and extra equipment.

The advertised drive-away prices apply to vehicles in standard Acorn Brown paint purchased and delivered by December 31, 2026, or while stocks last. Government, fleet and rental buyers are excluded.

READ MORE: 2026 Leapmotor B05 Priced for Australia: Rear-drive electric hatch arrives to challenge MG4 Urban and BYD Dolphin
READ MORE: Leapmotor B10 plug-in priced for Australia: Compact SUV matches electric sibling on dollars, has much longer claimed range
READ MORE: 2026 Leapmotor B03X Brief Drive: Budget electric SUV keeps things simple and cheap

Listed prices before on-road costs are $26,990 for the Style and $30,990 for the Design LR. Optional paint costs another $990.

The B03X’s most direct rival is the similarly sized BYD Atto 2, which starts at $31,990 before on-road costs in Dynamic form and rises to $35,990 for the Premium.

That gives the entry-level Leapmotor a $5000 advantage on list price, while its $29,990 drive-away offer is $2000 below the BYD’s starting price even before registration, stamp duty and dealer delivery are added to the Atto 2.

However, the cheaper B03X Style also has less claimed driving range. Its 39.8kWh lithium iron phosphate battery delivers 292km on the WLTP test cycle, compared with 345km for both Australian Atto 2 variants. The Leapmotor Design LR’s 53kWh battery lifts its claim to 382km.

Another important competitor is the GWM Ora 5, which starts at $33,990 drive-away — $4000 above the B03X Style and matching the Design LR’s advertised price.

Buyers considering a larger small electric SUV also have options such as the Chery E5 and MGS5 EV. MG’s current October offer puts the MGS5 EV Essence 49kWh at $39,990 drive-away after cashback, $10,000 above the entry-level Leapmotor.

The B03X also competes for budget EV buyers with electric hatchbacks. BYD currently advertises its Dolphin Essential at $28,888 drive-away, illustrating how closely the new Leapmotor SUV is priced to smaller alternatives.

Known as the A10 in China, the B03X measures 4270mm long and 1810mm wide, with a 2605mm wheelbase. That makes it slightly shorter and narrower than the Atto 2.

Australian specifications differ from the early Chinese-market versions previously driven by EV Central, with the local announcement listing rear-wheel drive and substantially higher power outputs.

The Style produces 130kW and 200Nm, while the Design LR increases power to 145kW. Leapmotor quotes an identical 8.6-second 0–100km/h time for both variants.

Both have 11kW AC charging capability, while maximum DC charging rates are 100kW for the Style and 133kW for the Design LR.

Leapmotor claims a 30–80 per cent recharge takes approximately 16 minutes under optimal conditions. Both versions also offer vehicle-to-load functionality capable of supplying up to 3.3kW to external appliances.

Standard equipment includes a 14.6-inch touchscreen, an 8.8-inch digital instrument display, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, satellite navigation, wireless phone charging and automatic climate control.

The Style also includes cloth upholstery, a six-speaker audio system, LED headlights, roof rails, rear parking sensors and a reversing camera.

The $4000 step to Design LR buys an additional 90km of claimed range, along with 18-inch alloy wheels, synthetic leather upholstery, an electrically adjustable driver’s seat, heated front seats and a heated steering wheel.

It also adds a 12-speaker audio system, ambient lighting, front parking sensors and a 360-degree camera with an integrated dashcam recorder.

Seven airbags are standard across the range, as are autonomous emergency braking, adaptive cruise control, lane-keeping assistance, blind-spot monitoring and front and rear cross-traffic alert with braking assistance.

Practical features include 60:40 split-folding rear seats, a rear storage compartment and up to 1315 litres of cargo capacity with the rear seats folded.

The B03X is covered by a six-year/150,000km vehicle warranty and an eight-year/160,000km high-voltage battery warranty.

Leapmotor also lists eight years of roadside assistance and capped-price servicing, with service intervals of 12 months or 20,000km, whichever comes first.

The post Australia has a new electric SUV pricing benchmark: Leapmotor B03X arrives from $29,990 drive-away appeared first on EV Central.
